A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same HalluEntity research. Their complete main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and can be matched despite the changed title and layout.

before.justification: v2 reports original evaluations of five uncertainty methods across 17 LLMs, dataset statistics, and linguistic error analyses.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds annotation-quality measurements and generator–proxy correlation results in Appendices A and B.

M1.justification: The FActScore-to-entity annotation pipeline, five uncertainty methods, and token-to-entity averaging remain unchanged. The expanded descriptions of manual verification and labeling conventions do not establish a changed procedure.

E1.justification: Appendix B adds biographies generated by open-source LLMs for proxy validation, extending the generator conditions beyond the original ChatGPT/GPT-3.5 corpus. The biography domain and entity-level hallucination task remain unchanged.

E2.justification: The benchmark retains Likelihood, Entropy, CCP, SAR, and Focus, and the plotted error analyses retain their comparators. The added proxy study uses existing methods and models. TSV is newly cited but explicitly excluded from evaluation.

E3.justification: v3 adds annotation assessment using segmentation similarity and label agreement on matching entities, plus Pearson-correlation comparisons across three target generators and seven scoring models. The original benchmark models, metrics, and hallucination-rate groups remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 provides linguistic, model-size, and hallucination-rate analyses but no quantitative annotation-quality or generator–proxy validation. Appendices A and B add both, substantially extending checks on two foundations of the study: label reliability and the use of proxy uncertainty scores.

E5.justification: Appendix A first reports three annotation runs on a random subset, Fleiss’s kappa across runs, and Cohen’s kappa between GPT-4o and verified labels, conditional on matching entities. The subset size is unspecified. This adds reliability reporting without establishing an increase in benchmark runs.

E6.justification: Tables 1–4 retain their numerical results. New findings include annotation Jaccard similarities of 0.813 and 0.945, kappa values of 0.984 and 0.940, and cross-model correlations in Tables 7–8. Section 5.3 also newly reports similar Entropy and Likelihood error trends.

T1.justification: Section 4 revises notation while retaining the scoring equations and entity averaging. The new proxy discussion supplies informal similarity assumptions and empirical motivation, without new formal definitions, derivations, proofs, or guarantees.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction’s contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims: introducing HalluEntity, benchmarking five methods across 17 LLMs, and identifying limitations of token-probability-based hallucination detection. The new title does not redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: v3 adds biography-only coverage and incomplete Wikipedia evidence as dataset limitations. It explains how multiple correct continuations can cause high uncertainty and argues for proxy validity through shared architecture, training sources, and observed correlations. These qualify and extend the retained interpretations.

D1.justification: v3 documents independent author verification, consensus resolution, external checking of conflicting annotations, and the pronoun-labeling convention. It identifies the original generator as GPT-3.5 and changes the stated MIT release status from forthcoming to released. These principally expand documentation of the existing dataset.

R1.justification: v3 adds Park et al. (2025), How to steer LLM latents for hallucination detection?, and mentions TSV among approaches lacking token-level scores. The broader related-work organization and novelty positioning remain unchanged.

P1.justification: v3 retitles the paper around HalluEntity, makes localized grammar and notation edits, aligns the annotation example with Figure 1, expands Limitations and Appendix A, and adds Appendix B. The main narrative and section order are largely retained.

P2.justification: Figure 2 replaces secondary-axis ratio bars with percentage annotations using the same data. Figures 5–6 are resized and placed side by side; Table 2 corrects its AUPRC heading; Table 6 is reformatted; and Tables 7–8 are added. The title page and publication headers also change.

improvement.justification: The annotation checks and proxy validation in Appendices A–B provide useful support absent from v2, while the expanded limitations and corrected table heading improve transparency. The gains remain limited: the repeated-annotation subset size is unspecified, and high score correlations do not directly establish equivalent hallucination-detection accuracy. The original benchmark evidence and conclusions remain intact.
